title: Least Even Multiple
statement: Given a positive integer n, return the smallest positive integer that is a multiple of both 2 and n.

examples.why: 6 is already even, so it is its own answer.
9 is odd. Its first multiple, 9, is odd too; the next one, 18, is even.
Every integer is a multiple of 1, so the answer is just the smallest positive even number.

hints: Multiples of n are n, 2n, 3n, … Which is the first one that is even?
If n is even, n itself works. If n is odd, n is odd but 2n is even.
In general this is lcm(2, n) = 2n / gcd(2, n).

explain.intuition:
The answer must be a multiple of n, so it is one of n, 2n, 3n, …. If n is even, the first candidate already works. If n is odd, n fails but 2n is even, so it is the answer.

This is the least common multiple of 2 and n: lcm(a, b) = a · b / gcd(a, b). The parity check is that formula specialised to a = 2, where the gcd is either 1 or 2.
pitfalls: Always returning 2 · n. For an even n that is a multiple, but not the smallest one.
Computing a · b before dividing by the gcd in a general lcm. For large values the product can overflow; divide first.

solutions.title: Parity check
solutions.idea: An even n is its own answer; an odd n needs one doubling.

solutions.title: General lcm with gcd
solutions.idea: lcm(2, n) = n / gcd(2, n) · 2. The same code works for any pair of numbers.

followups: Return the smallest positive number divisible by every integer from 1 to k.
